title: Diversity and the Way We Collectively Create a Social Reality
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's talk highlights the importance of recognizing and embracing cultural differences in order to deepen our understanding of diversity and intercultural development within their community, Red Cedar Zen. By acknowledging that our perceptions and behaviors are shaped by culture from childhood, we can approach life with humility, curiosity, and openness to new perspectives, leading to greater compassion and understanding for ourselves and others. This realization is rooted in the idea that there is no single human nature, but rather diverse versions of humanness that respond differently to stress and fear, and that our brains are "sculpted" by culture from an early age.

sentences.text: Hi everybody, good evening.
Broadcasting this week from my dad's place in Seattle.
A couple of announcements, updates.
One is that the Samish campground people are pretty happy.
Their goal was to raise $30,000 to help replace lost income from the missed season.
I guess it'll be almost two whole missed seasons.
It seemed like a pretty modest goal, but they did that and they raised more like $50,000.
As a community, the board decided we definitely wanted to help, so we sent $1,000 as a community and I'm sure many of us made individual gifts too.
In the little online fundraiser, it was like a variety show: music and little speeches and talks and reminiscing.
I had a little talk in there, and bims that have very beautifully produced an entire sketch of their retreat life there.
It's really nice.
I just wanted you to know that we helped out.
I'm sure many of us did as well in other ways.
Another thing is the Sunday program.

We were realizing that it's nice to have Sundays to be outside in the summer, and so Chris will give the talk this Sunday and I'll give the talk next Sunday, June 6th, and then we'll send Zen Alive on summer vacation until September 16th.
That's another thing.
It's nice having some seasonal change in our schedule.
That might show up other places too, recognizing the seasons and how precious the different seasons are and how we can live in different ways in different seasons, as we should.
Seems like there was a third thing, but maybe it'll come to me later.
Tonight we arrive.
Sorry, I'm bouncing around a little bit here.
I'm on a couch.
The laptop's on the couch.
Anyway, we arrived tonight in my last talk based on the book Seven and a Half Lessons about the Brain by Lisa Feldman Barrett.

I really hope this has been helpful or interesting, this peek into my sense of what she's trying to say, trying to tie in something about Buddhism and something about why this stuff matters beyond just that it's interesting scientifically, but that it really does affect more than affect our world and ourselves and our societies, I think.
The last two chapters of the book are about the connected topics of diversity and the way we collectively create a social kind of reality.
The reality that we live in the middle of, that we kind of mistake for other kinds of reality.

The important thing that she makes about diversity, which is pretty interesting, is that from a neurological, brain-centered perspective that she's speaking from, we're actually even more different than we realize, in some ways much more different.

Especially since it turns out that many of us in the dominant culture have a tendency to either deny differences between peoples of other cultures, which is a unit of difference, not the only unit, but a unit of difference, or many of us in the dominant culture also have the more subtle and probably more common, amongst this group, tendency to kind of minimize differences, to really lean on our sort of universal common humanity, the way we think about it, so that we don't see where it can be a little blind to diversity in a well-meaning way: that we want to honor our commonality.
So I've been learning a bit about that.
It's a quality that some call minimization.
There's a way that we minimize cultural differences and minimize diversity.
Very well-meaning, as I say, common probably among liberal types.
One place I've been learning about this is at Mindfulness Northwest.
We've decided that this is really important, serving all the different communities we're trying to serve, and equally important here at Red Cedar Zen.
But there, it's a little more of a business, so there's a little more money and organizational whatever.
So we hired an expert to help us learn about this and to help us find out, each of us, where we're at with our understanding of diversity and intercultural development, is what they call it.
They have a model with five stages in it of intercultural development.
So this is pretty helpful, I think.
The model has these five stages.
The first, lowest stage is denial, which is pretty self-explanatory.
Can be negating the entire idea that it even matters to care about diversity, or it can be negating the thought that there is any diversity.
So there's a denial level.
The second level is polarization, a really strongly us-versus-them viewpoint.
And probably most often that our culture is better than anyone else's, but it can also be flipped the other way.
Sometimes that shows up in kind of like hippie culture: other cultures are better than ours.
So polarization, one group is definitely better.
The third level that I want to talk about a little bit is called minimization.
In Mindfulness Northwest, working with this expert, we each took a little test, a little assessment of our stage of cultural development, intercultural development.
And this third, middle stage of minimization is where most of the 10 of us landed, including me.
So here's a definition of minimization.

*It's an orientation that highlights cultural commonality and universal values and principles that may also mask deeper recognition and appreciation of cultural differences.* *An orientation that highlights cultural commonality and universal values and principles that may also mask deeper recognition and appreciation of cultural differences.*
What's interesting about this is that mostly it sounds pretty good, right?
To us and to me anyway, to highlight cultural commonality and universal values and principles.
That sounds pretty good.
But it has this shadow side of masking, of strengthening blind spots, of not noticing differences that are actually there.
And it's a multiple choice assessment, which has been validated in various ways.
So it's apparently pretty effective.

And what I noticed when I was answering the questions on the assessment that led me to find out I'm in this category of minimization is that there were quite a few along the lines of, "Would you say your culture is better or worse than other cultures at...?"
And then there'd be a different thing.
There are several questions like that.
Is our culture better or worse than other cultures at, for example, raising children?
Communicating?
Various things cultures do.
And people do, right?
Each time I had one of these questions, I noticed I went through a similar thought process.
There's something like, hmm, well, there are people in my culture who are really good at that, and there are people in my culture who are really bad at that, poor at that.
So that's got to be true for every other culture, right?
Humans vary.
We're all on different spectrums and stuff.
So how could one culture on average really be better than the other culture?
And so I picked the middle choice.
It's like a strong "we agree, disagree," five choices.
So I picked the middle one.
And it does have a kind of ring of truth and logic to it, doesn't it?
And yet it's a certain kind of logic.
It's the logic of minimization.
This kind of losing the forest for the trees kind of thing: noticing differences.
So the next two levels up, for completeness, are acceptance, which is *an orientation that recognizes and appreciates patterns of cultural differences and commonality in one's own and other cultures.
An orientation that recognizes and appreciates patterns of*
difference, cultural difference, and commonality in one's own and other cultures.
The fifth, the top level, the best level, is adaptation: an orientation that can shift cultural perspective and change behavior in culturally appropriate and authentic ways.
Adaptation.
An orientation that can shift cultural perspective and change behavior in culturally appropriate and authentic ways.
This was a bit painful for me, actually, to learn from this assessment and this model, in this framework at least, that I'm not as accepting or as adaptable to other cultures as I like to think I am.

Although, when I was talking to the consultant about it, he cheered me up a little bit by saying, well, yeah, but you are at least in the upper half of the minimization of my score, so I almost made it to acceptance.
This is not to say that reality is ever one-dimensional and that I'm not accepting and adaptable.
But maybe this mindset of minimization is much stronger than I realized, and I was doing it without realizing I was doing it.
That's one of the big themes in the neuroscience book, that we think we know what's going on, and a big theme in Buddhism, too, right?

There are various ways we can look at our perceptions and our behavior and our assumptions that help us to realize the rest of our mind is moving us in certain ways that we might not be that aware of, and so these kinds of tools are helpful that way.
What Dr.
Barrett says about cultural differences from a neurological perspective seems to match what I'm learning from this five-stage model.
She says it's not just that there are different versions of the same human, like small differences, minimization, right?

Actually, the way our brains get sculpted by culture and experience from childhood, it's more accurate to say there are different versions of humanness, and she says flat out there is no single human nature.
That's her scientific perspective.
Her biggest example in the chapter is to look at patterns of reaction, not just attitude but physiological, whole-body patterns of reaction to fear and stress, to threat, basically.

As we well know, because it gets talked about so much, humans in our culture, when we get frightened or go into some kind of threatened state, can very quickly go into a fight or flight type response.
It's usually explained as deeply biological, and it is biological and neurological too.
But the way it's explained, I'm now learning, is a little off.

It's explained as a system where part of your brain, previously we heard it called the lizard brain, but we learned from her that's not quite right, but our brain makes an assessment that there's something frightening or dangerous going on that may exceed our resources to deal with it.
It's very fast.
We're primed for this threat response, we're told.

When it kicks off, it initiates a really fast chain of hormonal and physical changes, priming your body so you can fight, hit harder, bring all the blood out to the limbs, or run faster to flee and get away.
So you can deal with it, right?
But what she points out is that's not the universal human response.
That's the response of the dominant culture that runs the show, that does the science and talks about these things.
Even there, it turns out there's a lot more nuance to it.
It turns out that this fight or flight framework is also a very male framework, even within the dominant culture.
Once women scientists got interested, they said, well, there's more to the story than that.
But what she says in here is that there are also culturally sculpted brains, other kinds of humans that don't respond that way at all.
The example she gives is the traditional people of Bali, and some other Indonesian area cultures: when they feel threatened or afraid, they relax, chill out and go to sleep.
Totally different.
In the neurology, it's different.
The way they describe their emotions and response is different.
Of course, language is different.
But language, she says in here, is not just that we have different words for the same experience.
It's actually that we have very different kinds of experiences.
So the diversity she describes goes much deeper than we realize.
It's not just different versions of me; it's other types of people altogether.
Now, when we say, oh, it's only human, or that's how the human mind and body works, we're minimizing those differences, or missing the boat.
It would be much more accurate to say something like, well, this is how the kind of human I ended up being, the humans I hang out with, respond to stress or cope with this, that, the other.
This is our human nature.
But actually, other types of humans respond differently.
And there are other kinds of human nature.
So there is, she tells us, one brain architecture that underlies all these different minds, assuming that our mind comes from our brain.

Since that one architecture is so complex, remember, such a massive network, more than a billion neurons able to assemble themselves and interact with each other in trillions of patterns, it's massive.
It's amazing that could all be in your head, in every one of our heads.
There is this underlying architecture, but the way this massive architecture gets tuned up and refined and changed as we grow up.
Remember how it actually gets quite a bit pruned at the beginning, that we start out with more neurons than we end up needing as adults.

The brain also has an evolutionary interest in efficiency, figuring out, well, it doesn't really figure out, but we say this figuring out, how it can pattern itself to efficiently keep us alive and interact with our environment.
And our environment is a cultural environment.
That's the other point she's making.
It's not just a physical environment.
Culturally, we've invented an entire complex world, and we take the made-up things in our complex world to be very real.
So our brain evolves to deal with that particular world, and you end up with basically different humans, same species but very different.
And yet the brain is so amazing that at the same time it retains all kinds of redundancy and complexity and flexibility to handle variation within that world, too.
Remember how she said in some [unclear: "chat"] many chapters ago that there's never even just one neural pathway to do any one action.

I was so fascinated by that: if you bend your finger one time and then bend your finger another time, different neurons are involved, so that if something goes wrong, you can still bend your finger and onward and upward from there.
And one point she makes about all this that really sticks with me from a social justice perspective.

There's a lot of social justice perspectives that come straight out of this neurological information, but was that the children of immigrants, their brains have to work extra hard because they have to be able to function in both the culture of their parents and in the culture of the surrounding dominant culture, when they go off to school or down to the corner store or need to translate for their parents.

Razal and I were at Target the other day and the family ahead of us were Hispanic, maybe Mexican family, and the mom was trying to understand about returning something because she thought that the price could reduce because she saw a flaw on it, and her daughter had to translate and go back and forth.
It's just shown me to realize now what's not just knowing two languages, it's navigating two cultures.
So these kids' brains have to be tuned and pruned to the dual purpose, so that's less efficient, more expensive, more complex.
One more barrier for immigrant kids, in addition to all the socioeconomic factors and layers of racism and prejudice they have to navigate every day.
Even at that level, they have to work twice as hard, right?
But now we find out their brains are also working twice as hard to navigate this multicultural life they're in the middle of.
We've all experienced that, probably, if you've ever traveled anywhere.
If you're a native English speaker and you've ever had a chance to travel somewhere that's surrounded by non-English-speaking culture, it's really interesting, isn't it?
But it's also exhausting.

It's interesting to realize it's not exhausting just because it's confusing and you couldn't figure out how to ask where's the whatever, but it's extra exhausting because your brain is literally trying to reconfigure, rewire itself to cope with a different cultural situation where you can't take things for granted and run all the neural pathways that you've already established that happen so automatically.
It's big things and little things.
In our culture for "come here" we make this gesture, and in Asian cultures it's this gesture.

I remember being in the airport in Korea on the way to Japan, and one of the people made this gesture, and it took me an extra little moment of intense concentration to figure out that that meant "come here," which would have been so automatic, right?
It was like, what does that mean? [unclear: "something in her ear"] when she's trying to say something, she's looking at me funny.
It's not a big deal, she would have eventually said "come here please" in English probably for me, but there's that extra little bit of neurological processing that had to happen for me.

So it's all really interesting, but also in the end it really does all matter because it's how we're constructing reality: our ability to make up and believe, and our socially created, culturally created experience.
It even includes our inner experiences, the emotions we feel and the thoughts we think we have.
They're being kind of like selected from a cultural menu and they're bound by language, which makes perfect sense.

I think about this a lot from Buddhist psychology: that the very way we understand the world in concepts also limits the way we can perceive the world, because we've only perceived the things that we conceptualize.
It's one of the wonderful things about meditation, isn't it, that sometimes we have a bit of a glimmer of the non-conceptual world, so beautiful and interesting beyond the limits of language.
But we mostly live in this relative world informed by our language and bound by it.
Other cultures have a different version of all this, right?

But then the deeper dive diversity point she's making is it's not just that they have different names for the same feelings, they literally have different feelings, not their own version of this, their own version of that.
I'm sure there's tremendous overlap, probably everyone has a version of anger and everyone has a version of fear, even though they call it different things, but different versions.
And probably other emotions that we don't even feel because we can't know about them, we don't have the framework.

It's kind of like the one in language acquisition that was in earlier chapter two, that newborns are primed to hear all kinds of sounds, but that's quickly pruned down to the sounds that predominate in your language, and so it gets a lot harder to hear different sounds that aren't in your language.

This shows up too in the way the early Buddhist scholars and practitioners were trying to figure out their world and name their world in the interests of reducing suffering, right, in the interests of really understanding how the mind works.

The early Buddhists made up all kinds of maps of the mind, maps and descriptions of the different kinds of experiences you can have and how they hook together and how they affect you, and which kinds of mental experiences lead to more suffering and which lead to less suffering.
One of the root meanings of the word dharma, which is a multi-level word, is that a dharma is a moment of experience, like a unit of experience.
The different schools of early Buddhism set about slicing and dicing these different kinds of experiences and came up with very specific lists.
As you know, Buddhism is famous for its lists, so these are really important lists.
This is the system sometimes called abhidharma, abhidharma.
What's important about these lists is that they define reality in yet another way, yet another way of defining reality.
The early Buddhists said all the experiences you can possibly have ever are examples of each of these different kinds of things on these lists.

One of the most popular lists is a list of 51 different dharmas, and this is the list that Yogachara Buddhism adopted, which we've talked about Yogachara Buddhism before, remember the system with the storehouse consciousness that also seems to line up with some of the depths of neuroscience.
So anyway, I thought it'd be fun just for a kind of flavor to share with you a little bit about this list of 51 dharmas, because we're in this tradition that has some reference to this.
So the 51 dharmas are organized into six different categories.
I'm not going to read them all because you never remember, but I thought I'd give you a sampling.
I'll tell you what the categories are and just a few examples in each category.
It's pretty interesting actually.
First category are the omnipresent factors, mental factors that are happening all the time.
A few examples are attention, feelings, and perception.
These things are always happening.
So these are examples of experiences you can have.
You can have an experience of attention, an experience of feeling, an experience of perception.
And it's more multi-layered than that but close enough.
The next category is there are five object contingent factors.
So, factors that arise contingent on other mental objects.
A few of those are determination.
That's a mental experience you can have that's contingent: you're determined about something.
Mindfulness: you're mindful of something.
Concentration: concentrated on something.
And then there are 11 wholesome mental factors you can experience.
So this is the good stuff.
Here's a few examples.
Energy is a wholesome mental factor.
Ease and carefulness is another one.
There's 11 of them.
And then the next category is the six major afflictions.
We've heard of the major afflictions before.
In this list there are six.
Here's a few of them: pride, ignorance, and doubt.
And you better believe greed, hatred, and ignorance are on there too.
I already mentioned ignorance.
So there's six major afflictions.
That's really important for the relieving of suffering, to understand this kind of stuff.
And the way they organize it: there are factors that are always there.
There are factors that are contingent on things.
There are factors that are wholesome.
There are major afflictions that are unwholesome.
And then, I'm sorry to say, the largest group, the longest category of these 51, is the 20 secondary afflictions.
Here's a few examples: envy, deceitfulness, agitation, and forgetfulness, or also mindlessness.
And there's quite a few more, 20 of those.
Seven deadly sins are in there, I'm sure.
And then the last category is four leftovers.
They didn't know what to do with them.
These are the indeterminate factors, and they're kind of interesting.
I'll tell you all four.
One is regret.
Couldn't figure out what to do with regret.
Is it wholesome?
Is it unwholesome?
Who knows what regret's about?
I'm sure there's more than that known about it.
Another is sleepiness, the way we check out.
And there's two about thought, which I never did learn about: initial thought and sustained thought.
Point being that here's a framework, here's a cultural set of beliefs, maybe deeper than beliefs, a framework that was derived from many hundreds, maybe thousands of years of meditation practice.
But a framework, nonetheless, fascinating and important.
And I'm not knocking the system.
I think models are great.
But now you have to wonder, in light of what Dr.

Barrett is sharing, if the minds of Indian meditators from the second and third century BC, when we think this was put together, maybe the first century BC, are the minds of those ancient Indian meditators really the same kinds of minds that we have ended up with here today?
There's certainly a lot of overlap, and most of the mental factors, when I read through these kinds of lists, make total sense.
Some I'm a little confused by, or they make little sense, more of a stretch, but exploring them is revealing and interesting.
It's really food for thought, isn't it?
Because we have our model, whether we know it or not, right?
We have our ways that we describe our experience that we take to be just how it is.
But actually, it's a neurologically derived system.
It's a model that we ended up with, perhaps from the way our brain was pruned and tuned.
And it's complicated, of course, because our brain is so massive.
And yet there's this material physical basis to it all, which is comforting to us, I think, because we believe so much in the material.

But what I've appreciated about these seven and a half lessons about the brain is the ways it just shows us again and again and again, in a really scientifically powerful way, that our projections are simplistic, our beliefs are a bit suspect, and our assumptions about who and what we are are shaky at best.
And that's about ourselves.
Then our assumptions about others have really got to be off the charts wrong.
And then further, our assumptions about reality itself, and the things that we perceive, are not necessarily right.
We learned that the brain is generating reality in a controlled hallucination, and that our eyes are not windows of the soul, like little clear windows that our brain can see through, right?
Brain's in a dark place.
But light sensors, they get interpreted, and predicted with, predicted about even.
Sometimes what we're seeing is not even what's coming in as photons yet.
It's what our brain thinks we're about to see, so that we can efficiently go about the business of staying alive.
So to me, this all adds up to a really strong encouragement that on the one hand, we need to expand the bumper sticker wisdom of "don't believe everything you think."
It goes much deeper than that, right?
Don't believe everything you see, either, or hear, or believe.
Don't even believe the ways you describe and categorize reality.
It's not exactly the way you think it is.
Not totally wrong, but never quite right.

So I just think it adds up to a powerful encouragement to be humble, to be curious, to really listen deeply, and then to listen again, to keep learning and notice the places we're stuck, with the support of our friends.
So it's wonderful we have something like Sangha, to help us question our assumptions.
And when there's suffering, it's not a problem to solve, but a really valuable piece of information.
It's yet another way that we've misunderstood and misperceived who and what we are and what the universe really is.
An opportunity.
So we can, Shantideva anticipated this, right, and all of his wonderful verses about thanking the people that are mean to you, and all that stuff.
It's like, these are our teachers, to help us realize what Dr.
Barrett's trying to tell us in this book about our brains.
And taking this on, this broader, more open, more curious, less sure of ourselves way of living, isn't just a nice thing to do, right?
It isn't just a way to reduce our own suffering, even though it clearly does do that, definitely.
But this is really [unclear: "how we say of all beings"].
And the examples of this not happening, of course, bombard us and surround us and always have.
But lately, right, the last few years, it seems like even more.
So not that this stuff's happening less, but maybe we're a little more aware of it.
So I'm sorry to put something yucky in your head, but I want to give a specific example.
One more specific example.
We have plenty of them, I know.
But I read yet another news story today about police aggression against a black or brown person, a man.
In this one, the police, forget where it happened, North Carolina, maybe, can't remember where it happened.
But in this one, the police are responding to a complaint about a fight with weapons at a trailer park.
So that's some significant call.
They get to the trailer park and bang on someone's door.
According to the police, they had good reason to pick that particular door.
According to the family affected, there was no reason whatsoever for them to bang on it.
A 26-year-old man opens the door and wants nothing to do with the police.
For good reason, really, right?
We white people reading all these stories can get it on a certain level.
But imagine being in that position, being a black 26-year-old man living in a trailer park and the police are banging on your door.
So he refuses to cooperate.
In my notes, I couldn't help but put "cooperate" in quotes, because what a tricky use of the word, a very manipulative way of thinking about cooperating.
So anyway, he doesn't want to talk to the police or let them in or go outside with them whatsoever.
And so the police grab him, throw the cuffs on him, throw him in the police car and arrest him.
But here's the thing with this one: the cuffs are too tight.
They're cutting off the circulation in one of his hands.
He's telling them this, and they apparently ignore his complaints.
I read that there is a standard procedure you're supposed to follow if you put handcuffs on somebody, to make sure they're not too tight.
And that doesn't happen.
Handcuffs ratchet closed.
Not only can you put them on too tight initially and need to adjust them, but if you don't do an extra step to stop them, they can keep ratcheting tighter and tighter just from being jostled around.
So the person's hand hurts and goes numb for the 45 minutes or so that the cuffs are on him.
Then he's released because they have nothing whatsoever to charge him with.
Soon he starts having trouble with the circulation in this hand, in his fingers.
And eventually, this is the horrible part, the hand has to be amputated.
So a 26-year-old man now has one hand because of the choices these particular police officers made.
Because of how their brains perceive the situation of going to a trailer park to respond to this report of fighting, and the actions their brains have been trained to take, or chose to take.
Of course, it's very complicated, right?
A massive complex network, acculturated.
There's no simple summary here, even though I'm doing that anyway.
And maybe there's more to this story we don't know yet.
The family of the man filed a civil suit because apparently there was no action from the officials.
Maybe there was some underlying medical condition and it was partly bad luck that his hand responded so poorly to handcuffs.
But nonetheless, who's the one with one less hand?
But the good news is, of course, that these brains, like every other brain, can be trained differently, can change.
We can become more curious, more connected, more open-minded, more responsive.
We'll never know how these police officers, who were white, perceived this black man they arrested.
Maybe they couldn't really tell us themselves.
If we asked them, I don't know.

But something happened there between a small group of different brain operators, beings operated by their acculturated brains, in a situation of deeper diversity than any of us understand, and in a socially created world where we all have beliefs and understanding about what's supposed to be happening.
But our beliefs may not be right, or at least not in accord with the reality that we think they are.
So this stuff really does matter.
It's not just philosophy.
It's not just interesting, quirky science.
It's not just gee whiz.
This stuff has flesh-and-blood consequences in the world.
When we believe our perception and our views so rigidly, and get rigid, we cause harm.
Listen, we're closed.
We do a lot of damage.
And every one of us has done some damage, right?
Absolutely.
And plenty of healing too, of course.
So at last Sunday's program, we had a wonderful guest visitor.
I was lucky I got to be there.
Chris Forten from California, a student also of [unclear: "Normans"], gave the talk, and she read to us a modern Native American poem by Joy Harjo called "Rabbit Is Up to Tricks."
So I thought I'd close this last brain science talk with this poem.
It seems like it fits pretty well.
You can find this on the internet pretty easily.
Here's Joy Harjo's "Rabbit Is Up to Tricks."
*In a world long before this one, there was enough for everyone, until somebody got out of line.
We heard it was Rabbit, fooling around with clay and the wind.
Everyone was tired of his tricks and no one would play with him.
He was lonely in this world.
So Rabbit thought to make a person.
And when he blew into the mouth of that crude figure to see what would happen, the clay man stood up.*
*Rabbit showed the clay man how to steal a chicken.
The clay man obeyed.
Then Rabbit showed him how to steal corn.
The clay man obeyed.
Then he showed him how to steal someone else's wife.
The clay man obeyed.
Rabbit felt important and powerful.
The clay man felt important and powerful.
And once the clay man started, he could not stop.
Once he took that chicken, he wanted all the chickens.
Once he took that corn, he wanted all the corn.
Once he took that wife, he wanted all the wives.
He was insatiable.
He had a taste of gold and he wanted all the gold.
Then it was land and anything else he saw.
His wanting only made him want more.
Soon it was countries and then it was trade.
And the wanting infected the earth.*
*We lost track of the purpose and reason for life.
We began to forget our songs.
We forgot our stories.
We could no longer see or hear our ancestors or talk with each other across the kitchen table.
Forests were being mowed down all over the world and Rabbit had no place to play.
Rabbit's trick had backfired.
Rabbit tried to call the clay man back, but the clay man wouldn't listen.
And Rabbit realized he'd made a clay man with no ears.
Rabbit's trick had backfired.
He tried to call the clay man back, but when the clay man didn't listen, Rabbit realized he'd made a clay man with no ears.*
So we need our ears.
We also need to understand ears and brains, minds and hearts, right?
It's a much bigger system than just ears.
We certainly need to learn how to listen.
Thanks very much for listening to this talk and so many talks about the brain science book.
